RagShortTexts: The 13th-century coat of plates riveted shaped iron plates inside leather to counter heavy.

Variants.Content: Traditional mail hauberks gave poor protection against crushing warhammers and heavy crossbow bolts, which could drive rings into the flesh without cutting them. Armourers answered by developing the coat of plates, a garment in which overlapping iron plates were riveted to the inside of a stout canvas or leather surcoat. The hybrid design absorbed concussion and deflected points while leaving the torso free to move, and it prepared the way for the full plate harness of the later fourteenth century. Its cost put it within reach of wealthier knights and sergeants, and a good coat could be worth several months of a retainer's wages.

Armourers in Milan and Nuremberg now craft plates tailored to the body beneath velvet shells. Gilded rivets trace heraldic motifs across the chest, so the armor shows rank as well as protecting the wearer. A lord who commissions such a coat expects his plates to hold against a crossbow at close range and his household to see the expense.

A mace strike through plain mail shatters ribs without cutting the skin. Shaped iron plates riveted under the surcoat turn a spear point aside. Oil the rivets, check the straps before every breach, and keep the plates clean of mud so the leather does not rot where it sits against your chest.
